title: Why Does Your Stomach Growl?
description: Why does an empty belly rumble? Pip and Ray follow muscular waves through the gut. Feeding interrupts the fasting migrating motor complex; gut sounds can still happen after meals. Educational animation, not medical advice.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Grrrrrk... RAY! My belly just made a MONSTER noise!

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: That was not a monster. That was borborygmi. It is Greek for rumbling.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: It speaks muscle. Your gut is one long tube with walls of muscle... and those walls squeeze in waves.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Waves?! In my belly? What are they pushing?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Food, juice, and swallowed air. Every squeeze mixes and pushes them along... and the pushing makes the rumble.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: But why is it SO much louder when I am hungry?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: When your stomach has been empty for about two hours, special sensors in its walls trigger a cleaning wave... the migrating motor complex.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: A cleaning wave? My gut has a MAID?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Exactly! It sweeps leftover crumbs and mucus all the way down, so nothing piles up. And an empty tube cannot muffle the sound... so you hear it LOUD.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: So the growl is my gut vacuuming. Incredible!

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: The wave rolls for ten to twenty minutes, then comes back every hour or two... until you finally eat something.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Then I know exactly how to fire the maid. SNACK time!

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Feed it, and the cleaning wave pauses. Your gut still moves... but on the fed shift.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: My belly: rumbling since the ancient Greeks. SCIENCE!
